analysis.one_liner: Halted new endangered species protections and paid landowners when habitat designations lowered their land values.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to its Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have frozen the Interior Department's power to add species to the endangered list and to designate critical habitat until Congress reauthorized the Endangered Species Act. It also would have required the government to pay private landowners, on request, for any drop in market value when their land was designated critical habitat. Finally, it would have excused any federal action costing under $500,000 from the usual duty to avoid harming endangered species.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of farm, ranch, and development land would gain twice: no new critical habitat designations could lower their property values while the moratorium lasted, and any designation that did occur could trigger a taxpayer-funded payment for lost market value. Developers, timber, mining, and agricultural operators would benefit from the moratorium on new listings and from the exemption of projects under $500,000 from review under the Endangered Species Act [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It bars the Secretary of the Interior from listing any species as endangered or threatened, or designating any critical habitat, until the Act's next reauthorization [S2][S3].
It requires the government to compensate private landowners, on request, for any loss in the market value of land resulting from a critical habitat designation [S2][S3].

It limits the requirement that federal agencies avoid jeopardizing endangered species or their critical habitat to actions costing $500,000 or more, freeing smaller projects from that review [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the market-value compensation payments, and the public would bear the cost of a years-long freeze on protecting newly imperiled species and habitats, with no way to protect a species even in an emergency once the freeze took effect [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The moratorium is a blanket freeze: it would stop protection for every newly imperiled species, no matter how severe the situation, until Congress reauthorized the Act, which could take years [S2][S3].

Compensation would be an open-ended charge on taxpayers, and the certainty of having to pay landowners for designations would give the government a strong financial reason to avoid designating critical habitat at all [S2][S3].
The $500,000 spending threshold would exempt most routine federal actions from the duty to avoid harming endangered species, since the current rule applies regardless of expense [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compensation provision speaks to a real grievance: a critical habitat designation can lower a landowner's property value, and paying for that loss is a defensible response. But the bill couples it with a total moratorium on new species listings and a spending threshold that exempts most federal projects from review. The net effect is a multi-year suspension of endangered species protections, with the public bearing both the ecological loss and the bill for compensation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 1994, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison introduced the bill on September 22, 1994, for herself and Sen. Phil Gramm [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill had one cosponsor and no committee action, floor vote, or House counterpart action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed: existing endangered species protections and listing authority stayed intact, while landowners and resource developers gained no moratorium and no compensation. Nobody moved the law in either direction.

for.name: Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Texas Republicans; no votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large private landholders
industries.note: A moratorium on new listings and critical habitat designations removes the main regulatory limit on developing land that shelters endangered species, and compensation turns any future designation into a federal payment to the owner. The benefit to owners comes directly out of species protection and the public purse [S2][S3].

The bill is framed around farms and ranches, and a freeze on habitat designations plus market-value compensation shields ranchland values from habitat restrictions. Some smaller landowners would genuinely gain from compensation; the cost is shifted to taxpayers and to species protection [S2][S3].

Species listings and critical habitat designations frequently restrict logging and mining on both private and federal land; a moratorium on both removes that constraint until reauthorization, and the $500,000 exemption spares smaller federal actions from review entirely [S2][S3].
